planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep once soil has warmed well past 70°F, since this vigorous climbing sieva-type lima rots readily in cool, damp spring ground.

directions: Set a sturdy 6- to 8-foot trellis or pole at planting time, since this old South Carolina Lowcountry heirloom is a rampant climber that will not perform as a bush type. The small, flattened seeds are handsomely mottled brown-on-tan, giving the variety its name, and cook down tender with the rich, mild, buttery flavor Charleston cooks prize in a proper pot of butterbeans and rice. It sets pods steadily through the hottest, most humid weeks of a Gulf Coast summer when many snap beans have stalled, and because it flowers over a long season, regular picking at the green-shell stage keeps vines productive into fall. Save seed by letting some pods dry fully on the vine, since this open-pollinated heirloom breeds true.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well above 65°F; okra seedlings sulk and can rot in cool spring soil, so Gulf Coast gardeners generally wait until early-to-mid May.

directions: Bradley is a widely grown Deep South home-garden hybrid prized for smooth, spineless, dark green pods that stay tender well past the 3-4 inch stage, forgiving gardeners who miss a picking day or two in peak summer heat. Plants stay a manageable, well-branched height compared to rangy heirloom types, which makes hand-harvesting easier and keeps pods within easy reach all season. It sets pods heavily and continuously through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer, when many other vegetables shut down, and responds well to a side-dressing of nitrogen once plants begin flowering. Pick every day or two once pods start forming, since Bradley pods can pass tenderness quickly in hot weather.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after all frost danger is past and soil is warm; give vines a full summer since this long-season moschata needs 100+ frost-free days to fully cure.

directions: This Cherokee heirloom from the North Carolina and North Georgia mountains produces medium-sized, buff-tan skinned fruit with dense, deep orange, sweet-nutty flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata, it carries the family's excellent resistance to squash vine borer and better tolerance of humid, disease-pressured Southern summers than most Cucurbita pepo pumpkins. Let vines sprawl generously, since a single plant can cover a large area and set several fruit; harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail and stems have begun to dry and corky. Cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot, making it a reliable keeper crop for fall and winter kitchens.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this heirloom sets fruit well through Gulf Coast summer heat.

directions: This old Mississippi dooryard heirloom produces slender, tapered fruit that ripen from pale yellow-green through orange to bright red, with a medium heat similar to a cayenne. It was passed down among home gardeners specifically for pickling whole in vinegar brine, and the thin-walled pods also dry and grind well for homemade hot pepper flakes or vinegar-pepper sauce. Compact, heavily branched plants handle Deep South humidity and heat well and keep setting new pods through summer if picked regularly rather than left to fully color on the plant. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other annuum peppers by distance if you intend to save true seed.
